what: Brookfield Infrastructure Corporation owns essential infrastructure. It is the corporate share class of Brookfield’s infrastructure business, holding regulated utilities, gas pipelines, electricity transmission, data centres and midstream energy assets across several continents.
customers: Varies by asset: electricity and gas customers of its regulated utilities, energy producers using its pipelines, and technology companies leasing its data centre capacity.
money: Regulated electricity and gas distribution and transmission businesses.
Natural gas pipelines, processing and storage.
Data centres, towers and transport infrastructure.
moat: These are assets with regulated or contracted revenue, very long lives, and no realistic competition: nobody builds a second gas pipeline alongside an existing one or a competing electricity network. Revenue is typically inflation-linked by regulation or contract, which protects the real value of the cash flow over decades.
risks: Debt of $12.7B against $431.0M of cash is enormous relative to a $5.1B market value, and infrastructure is financed against contracted cash flow.
A trailing net loss of $252.0M — heavy depreciation on long-lived assets makes reported earnings unusable for this asset class.
Only one analyst covers the stock, with a $48.00 target, so there is almost no external scrutiny.
Rising interest rates hurt twice: they raise financing costs and reduce the present value of long-dated contracted cash flows.
The corporate structure and its relationship with the partnership make the economics harder to assess than an ordinary company’s.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $1.5B against a $5.1B market value, at about 3.5 times free cash flow, with EV/EBITDA of 6.1.
Revenue has grown strongly, from $1.6B in 2021 to $3.7B in 2025.
Regulated and contracted revenue with inflation linkage protects the real value of cash flow over decades.
Pipelines, electricity networks and similar assets have no realistic competition — nobody builds a second one.
Data centre demand is a genuinely new source of growth for infrastructure owners with power and land.
watch: Funds from operations per share and the contracted or regulated share of revenue. Reported earnings are meaningless here; contracted cash flow per share is the business.
view: Infrastructure of this kind is among the most defensible asset classes that exists, and the reason is physical rather than commercial. Nobody builds a second gas pipeline alongside an existing one, or a competing electricity distribution network, or a duplicate port. The assets last for generations, the revenue is set by regulation or long contract, and the pricing is usually linked to inflation. That combination protects real cash flow over decades in a way very few businesses can.

The accounting makes this hard to read and it is important not to be misled. A trailing net loss of $252 million reflects heavy depreciation on assets whose economic lives far exceed their accounting lives, plus project-level financing. The useful measures are funds from operations per share and the contracted share of revenue. Free cash flow of $1.5 billion against a $5.1 billion market value — about 3.5 times — is the figure that describes what the equity actually receives.

The structural weakness is leverage: $12.7 billion of debt against $431 million of cash. Infrastructure is financed against its contracted cash flow, which is a sound model while that cash flow is stable and refinancing is available, and the source of real fragility if rates rise sharply. Higher rates hurt these assets twice over, raising the cost of new capital and reducing the present value of long-dated cash flows already owned. That is why the whole sector derated when rates rose, and it was rational.

The newer development that genuinely helps is data centres: technology companies need power, land and connectivity, and infrastructure owners have all three. One analyst covering a $5.1 billion company is remarkable and means essentially nobody is examining this. At 6.1 times EV/EBITDA for regulated and contracted assets, the price is undemanding — provided the holder understands they are buying a leveraged infrastructure vehicle and judges it on funds from operations per share rather than earnings.
bull: Inflation-linked regulated and contracted revenue compounds while data centre demand opens a new growth channel, and falling rates lift long-dated cash flow values.
bear: Rates stay high against $12.7 billion of debt, refinancing costs rise faster than contracted escalators, and the equity absorbs it entirely.
